findings.problem: The Recommended Approach says the preset row's copied plugin list is kept in step by a small generator and that this is why the copy is generated rather than hand-maintained, but no generator exists anywhere in the plan: the layout lists only package.json, dsh.plugin.json, cordis.patch.yml, presets/gbrain-tools.patch.yml, lib/*, README.md and test/; Next Steps never writes one; and the only drift check named (Distribution Plan and Success Criterion 6) proves that dsh.plugin.json and cordis.patch.yml agree with dsh/lib/tools.js. presets/gbrain-tools.patch.yml, the file that actually carries the tools, is in neither the generator story nor any stated check, so the failure the generator was introduced to prevent (a future DSH release adds a tool and the preset silently loses it) is unguarded.
findings.remedy: Name the generator's path, add it to the layout and to Next Steps, and extend the --check (and Success Criterion 6) to cover presets/gbrain-tools.patch.yml and the README list, stating which artifact is the single source of truth.

findings.problem: Next Step 5 proves composition only for the Host patch (dsh --profile web --patch dsh/cordis.patch.yml --dump-config). The preset patch presets/gbrain-tools.patch.yml never gets a named target - which profile it belongs to and which preset declaration row it overrides or extends - and nothing in Next Steps or Success Criteria validates that it composes, that a preset carrying a copied plugin list still activates, or that the tools appear in a new session, although a preset revision is activated once and must be validated in a new session.
findings.remedy: Name the profile and the preset declaration id the preset patch targets, add the matching --dump-config run for the preset patch, and add a new-session activation check (the declared tools are present and match lib/tools.js) to Next Steps and Success Criteria.

findings.problem: No part of the design registers or syncs a user's project as a code source. The Distribution Plan's user flow ends at gbrain init, leaving an empty brain, and reindex-code is deliberately excluded from the tools with no replacement operator path and no cadence; incremental freshness after code edits, branch switches or a merged upstream release is unaddressed. Success Criterion 1 (a code-intelligence tool call returns a real answer from the Postgres brain) therefore has no reproducible path for anyone but the author's machine.
findings.remedy: Add the source lifecycle to the deliverable: how a project becomes a registered source, who runs sync/reindex and when (install step, hook, or scheduled job), and how staleness is surfaced; make it a step in the Distribution Plan and Next Steps so Criterion 1 is reachable by a reader.

findings.problem: Every request carries an explicit source_id, but the design never says who supplies it (the model or the Host), how a session's project maps to it, what happens for an unknown or foreign source, or whether a call may address a source outside its project. The helper calls gbrain as a trusted local caller, so gbrain's own scoping machinery (ctx.auth.allowedSources via sourceScopeOpts) is bypassed by construction, and Success Criterion 2's claim that the plugin adds no new path for a remote caller to reach a code read is asserted rather than demonstrated: the tool surface plus the per-user socket is that path, and no socket peer check, per-session authorization, or source allowlist is stated.
findings.remedy: Specify the routing and trust contract: where source_id comes from, the allowed set per session and its validation, the failure behavior for unknown or foreign sources, who may reach the socket, and the test proving a caller without the preset row cannot reach a code read.

findings.problem: The helper answers NDJSON requests over a Unix socket with one request type and Next Step 3 says to write the protocol, but the design fixes no framing or message-size limit, no request ids, no concurrency model, no timeout or cancellation rule, no error shape, no protocol version handshake, and no behavior while the helper is restarting. The fourteen tools, the health-check/restart requirement, and every test in Next Step 3 depend on those decisions.
findings.remedy: Specify the wire contract (protocol version, request/response schema, error envelope, size limits, timeouts, concurrency and cancellation, behavior during restart) as the first artifact, with a test per clause.

findings.problem: The design copies gbrain's op.description so tool selection stays prompt-engineered, but it never says how gbrain's own agent contract reaches the model as a tool result: the code/why/fix.next envelope, the [gbrain notice] and [AGENT] blocks, and exit 3 meaning stop and ask the user. A refused code read (Constraint 2) or a degraded search is the most likely first user-visible outcome of this plugin, and the design leaves it to be flattened into a generic error.
findings.remedy: Define and test the mapping from gbrain's refusal/degraded-result envelope to the DSH tool result - preserve code, why and fix.next, and surface the ask-the-user case - in tools.js or a shared adapter.

findings.problem: The pitch is no API key and no per-query process spawn, yet three exposed tools (query, recall, remember) depend on the brain's search mode and embedding provider, and possibly on a completion provider. The design never states which search mode or provider configuration the plugin assumes, what those tools do without one, or the search-mode confirmation gbrain's own install protocol requires before a default is accepted; the quickstart runs gbrain init --url ... and silently takes whatever default is applied.
findings.remedy: State the required or assumed search mode and provider configuration, the keyless degraded behavior per tool, and put the search-mode choice (with its cost matrix) into the install flow.

findings.problem: The Distribution Plan and The Assignment cannot run as written: the env file is written with only POSTGRES_PASSWORD, so GBRAIN_DATABASE_URL is never defined or exported, and the podman run mounts no volume, so the Postgres instance the design calls the single source of truth is destroyed with the container. The env file's permissions are also left to the umask while the design is careful about 0600 for the helper socket.
findings.remedy: Write the full connection URL (or its components plus the exported URL), add a persistent volume and a restart policy, chmod the env file to 0600, and verify the sequence end to end.

findings.problem: P4 and the eleven dsh-gstack skills depend on a gbrain binary on PATH being the fork's build, but the design never says how the fork's CLI is installed or linked under that name: the Distribution Plan invokes bare gbrain (which can be an upstream global install built from a different commit) while The Assignment uses bun src/cli.ts. The bundle install is likewise given as an unqualified path - plugin_manager install_bundle target <repo>/dsh - whereas the precedent the document cites is the family's link: spec form.
findings.remedy: State and verify the exact fork CLI command (bun link or a PATH shim) and the exact bundle install spec (for example link:<repo>/dsh), and use those forms in every recipe: install, assignment and CI.

findings.problem: backend-contract.js is a committed deliverable (D2, the layout, Next Step 6) whose entire specification is candidates in, results out, no raw SQL crossing the boundary. There is no operation list, no payload shape, no versioning or negotiation rule, no error behavior, and no statement of which side owns writes, and no consumer exists yet to validate it, so step 6's write and document it has no reviewable or testable output.
findings.remedy: Either specify the interface concretely (operations, payloads, version field and negotiation, errors, write ownership) or descope the file until the dsh-memory-evolve fork states what it needs, and in both cases name the test that would fail if the contract broke.

findings.problem: The helper is started, health-checked and restarted by the Host row, but the design never says who stops it, how a stale socket or an orphaned helper from a previous run is detected, what happens on plugin upgrade while an old helper is still listening, how version skew between plugin and helper is detected, or what removal does when plugin_manager remove_bundle leaves a daemon behind. Next Step 3 tests only that a dead helper is detected and restarted.
findings.remedy: Specify start, stop, upgrade, removal, stale-socket and version-skew behavior, and add tests for shutdown, removal, and a running helper from an older version.

findings.problem: Two of the tools write to the brain (put_page, remember) and the only stated constraint is the caller-supplied source_id, said to keep a decision about code out of a code mirror. There is no write policy: what may be written, where, how provenance is recorded, whether a model-initiated write needs consent, or how a misrouted write is undone - although the repository's own memory protocol treats automatic capture as opt-in and demands provenance.
findings.remedy: State the write policy for put_page and remember (allowed targets, provenance stamping, consent or approval behavior, and the reversal path) and add a test for a refused or misrouted write.

findings.problem: Success Criterion 1 makes the call traceable in the helper's log, but no log location, format, level, rotation, retention or redaction rule is specified, and the log records request parameters that include page and memory content from put_page and remember.
findings.remedy: Specify the log path, permissions, retention and redaction rules, and make the traceability criterion checkable against them.

findings.problem: The Operation Surface table lists twelve tools (code_def, code_refs, code_callers, code_callees, code_blast, code_flow, query, get_page, put_page, recall, remember, context_pack), but the same section says Fourteen tools, Success Criterion 6 says exactly the fourteen declared tools, and Next Step 4 says the fourteen tools. Nothing in the document names the other two.
findings.remedy: Fix the count or add the two missing tools, and derive the number from one artifact (lib/tools.js) so the prose, the manifest, the patches and the README cannot disagree.

findings.problem: Constraint 5 requires six free gates to stay green (verify, typecheck, test, test:e2e, ci:local, regen:all --check), but Success Criterion 3 defines done as only verify, typecheck and regen:all --check. Neither Criterion 3 nor the Distribution Plan's CI paragraph makes the new node --test dsh/test/ job a release condition, so the plan can satisfy its own definition of done while the only gate that runs the new tests is optional.
findings.remedy: State one gate list - the six commands plus the new dsh test job and its runner - and use it verbatim in Success Criterion 3 and the CI plan.

findings.problem: The design puts a node --test dsh/test/ job into the gbrain repo's own gates, an edit to upstream-owned CI configuration, while P3 promises no edits to upstream-owned files beyond a handful of small well-marked insertions and Success Criterion 4 requires that no upstream-owned file carries a behavioural change. Workflow files are exactly where upstream churn and merge conflicts concentrate, and Criterion 5's no-conflict merge promise has to survive that edit.
findings.remedy: Put the job in a new workflow file owned by the fork and name it, or state explicitly that a workflow edit is an accepted cost and show how it survives an upstream merge.

findings.problem: P1 says the native surface is a Host row that publishes an engine service plus a tool surface, but the Recommended Approach puts every tool in the preset row and quotes the wyrmbrain precedent NO TOOL IS REGISTERED HERE, AND THAT IS THE POINT for the host row. A reader approving P1 would expect the tools on the Host row.
findings.remedy: Restate P1 to match the placement decision (Host row publishes the engine service and the backend contract only; the preset row carries the tools), or change the placement.

findings.problem: Approach A is labelled chosen, mechanism corrected, while its body still describes the literal in-process Node import of gbrain subpaths including ./pglite-engine - an import Constraint 1 says fails under DSH's Node and a subpath D3 rules out (PGLite out of scope entirely). The runtime actually recommended (D4's resident Bun helper over NDJSON) is what Approach B describes, and the document says both that A was chosen and that B is where the design landed.
findings.remedy: State one chosen shape (Host row supervising a resident Bun helper), mark A, B and C as chosen or rejected accurately, and remove ./pglite-engine from the reused subpath list.

findings.problem: The helper listens over a Unix socket at a per-user path, while Open Question 4 makes database_url a per-profile value supplied from the profile patch. Nothing defines what happens when a second profile with a different database_url starts: a second helper on a different socket, a refusal, or silent reuse of the first helper - in which case profile B queries profile A's brain.
findings.remedy: Key the helper and its socket by database_url (or by profile) and define the multi-profile and multi-database behavior, including the error when a running helper serves a different database.

findings.problem: Success Criterion 4 checks additivity with git diff origin/master --stat, but the document elsewhere names upstream as the remote holding upstream gbrain (master and upstream/master are the same commit; Criterion 5 uses git merge upstream/master) and origin as the fork's own remote. Diffing origin/master against the branch compares the fork to itself and is vacuous.
findings.remedy: Diff against upstream/master, naming the configured remotes, so the additivity criterion actually measures divergence from upstream.

findings.problem: Constraint 6 says the mode writes down that gbrain must not be added as a preset row and explains it with the rule that a profile row claiming a serverName twice fails to load - but the Recommended Approach adds presets/gbrain-tools.patch.yml, which is a preset row. As written the constraint forbids the design's own central artifact; the prohibition in fact targets an MCP mount row, which the sentence never says.
findings.remedy: Reword Constraint 6 to name the forbidden row precisely (an MCP or mount row claiming gbrain's serverName) and state that the tools declaration row is a different kind of row.

findings.problem: The resident helper couples us to gbrain's external boundaries instead: the documented CLI, or the exported subpaths - an unresolved either/or in the paragraph that justifies the whole runtime choice - even though a long-lived engine connection with per-call source routing can only come from the exported subpaths, which is the subject of Open Question 2.
findings.remedy: Choose the exported-subpath import, with the relative-import fallback already noted, and delete or scope the CLI alternative so the merge-cost argument rests on one boundary.

findings.problem: Next Step 7 commits to building the typed planAdvisory seam and the external advisory kind that returns no advisory available until dsh-advisory-core lands, and Open Question 5 concedes the target is bootstrapped only (an AGENTS.md and no application code). The two named uses are speculative, and this is effort spent on an interface for an unbuilt component in a wave whose stated objective is minimal divergence from upstream.
findings.remedy: Descope the seam from this wave (the plugin already carries no second-opinion logic), or gate it explicitly as a follow-up that lands together with dsh-advisory-core and a stated first use case.

findings.problem: The go/no-go check in Next Step 1 and The Assignment is bun src/cli.ts code-callers performSync with no --source (only the earlier sync names --source dsh-gbrain), so on failure the reader cannot tell a refusal (Constraint 2's expected negative) from an unscoped read that returns nothing. The single highest-value hour in the plan would produce an ambiguous result.
findings.remedy: Pin the source explicitly (--source dsh-gbrain, or record which resolution tier bound it), state the exact expected refusal text, and record both the success and the refusal output as the decision evidence.

findings.problem: The new top-level dsh/ tree sits outside the repository's own test discovery - scripts/run-unit-shard.sh discovers tests with find test -name '*.test.ts' - and the module-size and coverage accounting are scoped to src/ and test/, so the promise that the free tests stay green says nothing about the new code, and the design never says which gate owns dsh/ or whether its tests are counted anywhere.
findings.remedy: State which repository gates inspect dsh/ (and any exclude or include edits needed), where the new tests are counted, and prove bun run test, verify and typecheck on the branch after dsh/ lands.
